AGE-FRIENDLY BANGOR: LOOKING BACK, MOVING FORWARD 
Bangor Livable Communities Committee | 2018 Action Plan Review 
The 2018 plan was a three-year roadmap built around eight domains of livability. Today we are asking: What did we accomplish? What is still unfinished? 
What has changed—and what should matter next? 
STATUS KEY:  ✓ Accomplished    → In progress / ongoing    ○ Not accomplished    ? We don’t know yet 
 
OUTDOOR SPACES & BUILDINGS 
Make public places easier to use for people of all abilities. 
2018 focus: Add rest/way stations; improve winter sidewalk access; ensure City 
facilities reflect accessibility needs. 
Progress: City walking audit (141 responses) documented sidewalk and crossing 
barriers. Parks/trails accessibility audit led to Kenduskeag Trail ADA benches, 
signage, crossing work and bridge assessment. New/expanded sidewalks and 
paths, snow-clearing changes, Complete Streets/Safe Streets work, ADA 
Transition Plan funding, and 2026 threshold ramps continue. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next Iteration: What are today’s highest-priority accessibility and visibility 
gaps?  
 
 
 
TRANSPORTATION 
Improve the ways people move around Bangor. 
2018 focus: Support transit and mobility partners; improve downtown access; 
advance Complete Streets and safer walking/biking. 
Progress since 2018: Community Connector moved to fixed stops and added a 
rider app, bus bike racks, ticket vending and electric-bus infrastructure. 
BACTS/DOT partnerships include Complete Streets, signal management, traffic 
calming and mobility planning. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next Iteration: What still limits reliable, independent mobility, especially for 
people who do not drive?  
HOUSING 
Improve housing options, quality, and the ability to remain at home. 
2018 focus: Participate in housing planning; connect residents to home-
repair/tax-relief resources; promote minimum housing quality. 
Progress since 2018: Universal-design elements are being incorporated into 
Grandview planning and pre-approved plans. Rehab and weatherization 
programs help prevent displacement. Zoning changes expanded housing choices 
through LD 2003, co-living, boarding homes, manufactured housing and 
supportive housing. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next Iteration: How do we make universal design, visitability and aging in place 
routine rather than exceptional?  
 
 
 
SOCIAL PARTICIPATION 
Make community activities accessible, affordable, and welcoming. 
2018 focus: Increase awareness of activities; expand opportunities for 
participation; reduce barriers created by mobility or access. 
Progress since 2018: Jane’s Walk, Sidewalk Art Festival, First Friday Art Walk, 
expanded parks/trails, community gardens, public art and partner programming 
create more gathering opportunities. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next iteration: Do opportunities translate into belonging? Who is still isolated or 
unable to participate? 
RESPECT & SOCIAL INCLUSION 
Strengthen inclusion, intergenerational connection, and volunteerism. 
2018 focus: Increase awareness of volunteer needs; create ways for residents of 
different ages and backgrounds to participate together. 
Progress since 2018: Community-led events, public art, Bangor Beautiful 
projects, accessibility work and partnerships show strong civic energy. Physical-
access work has expanded, but broader visitability and everyday social inclusion 
remain unfinished. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next iteration: What would a more neighborly Bangor look like? How do we 
make it easier to offer help, ask for help, and include people across ages and 
abilities? 
 
 
 
 
CIVIC PARTICIPATION & EMPLOYMENT 
Help older residents contribute through work, service, and civic life. 
2018 focus: Connect skilled volunteers to meaningful roles; support technology 
skills; identify resources for people returning to work. 
Progress since 2018: City and partner initiatives include internships, career 
exploration, public-service pathways, volunteer efforts and community-led 
events. We have limited evidence of a coordinated system matching people who 
want to help with places they are needed. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next iteration: “I have two hours and want to be useful.” Where do I go? What 
would everyday helpfulness and meaningful civic participation look like?
Source: City of Bangor Livable Communities Action Plan (July 2018) | Working handout for plan review 
COMMUNICATION & INFORMATION 
Make community information easier to find and accessible in multiple formats. 
2018 focus: Create a coordinated way to share activities/resources; connect 
residents to existing information sources and services. 
Progress since 2018: Digital tools and public information expanded through 
transit tracking, online portals, GIS/parcel tools and partner communications, 
but information remains spread across organizations and systems. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next iteration: Can people easily find help, activities, transportation and 
volunteer opportunities in formats they can use? 
 
 
COMMUNITY & HEALTH SERVICES 
Connect residents to services while identifying genuine gaps. 
2018 focus: Promote existing community resources; improve access to health 
services; fill gaps without duplicating what already exists. 
Progress since 2018: City and partners continue CDBG/social-service support, 
Shelter Plus Care, warming-shelter support, Public Health capacity and a broad 
regional network of health, aging and social services. 
Status:  ☐ ✓   ☐ →   ☐ ○   ☐ ?     Still relevant?  ☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Reframe 
Next iteration: Are remaining problems service gaps, access gaps, or 
navigation/connection gaps?

urgent?

Bangor Livable Communities 
Age-Friendly Plan Update: Discussion So Far 
Working summary of community discussions | September 11 and September 25, 2026 
Cross-Cutting Themes Emerging Across Both Meetings 
Access Connection Participation 
Can people physically get where they 
need to go, enter spaces, use public 
infrastructure, and find the 
information they need? 
Once people can get there, do they 
have opportunities to know others, 
share experiences, and feel that they 
belong? 
Can residents contribute, volunteer, 
help neighbors, and take part in 
shaping community life? 
Human connection as community infrastructure 
Across the discussions, participants repeatedly returned to the idea that a livable community is not only one where services 
are available. It is also one where people have regular opportunities to know one another, share experiences, offer help, and 
feel that they belong. 
Food → meals → gathering → relationships → volunteering → public space → belonging 
A useful frame for the updated plan 
The first meeting largely asked: “Can people access and move through the community?” The second meeting added another 
question: “Once people can get there, what helps them connect with other people?” Together, these discussions suggest a 
simple frame for future work: 
ACCESS + CONNECTION + PARTICIPATION 
September 11, 2026: Access, Communication, and Getting Around 
The first working session focused primarily on Communication, Transportation, and Accessibility/Public Spaces. The 
discussion emphasized the practical experience of moving through Bangor and being able to access places, information, and 
services. 
Communication 
• Develop a clearer communication plan for Livable Communities work and opportunities. 
• Consider how residents learn about services, activities, events, and ways to participate. 
• Make information easier to find and easier to use, particularly for people who may not rely on digital channels. 
Transportation and Access 
• Continue community walk audits and use them to identify barriers and priorities. 
• Improve crosswalk visibility and accessibility, including consideration of light-up crosswalks. 
• Address pedestrian push buttons that are difficult to see or locate and review whether crossing times are adequate. 
• Review placement of accessible parking spaces, sidewalk ramps, curb cuts, and their relationship to crossings and 
lighting. 
• Review the proximity of bus stops to accessible/ADAPT residential locations. 
• Review bus stop schedules near PJCC and explore shuttle options. 
Community Connection 
• The idea of a “Good Neighbor Day” emerged as an early example of creating intentional opportunities for neighbors 
to meet, connect, and help one another.
Bangor Livable Communities | Working Discussion Summary | September 2026 
September 25, 2026: Food, Connection, Volunteerism, and Social Space 
The second session moved organically across several domains. What began as a discussion about nutrition and health 
became a broader conversation about how communities create connection, belonging, and opportunities for people to help 
one another. 
Community & Health Services 
• Discussion began with the statewide Nourish ME initiative and the concept that “food is medicine.” 
• Participants connected nutrition to the broader gaps-in-care conversation: health is influenced not only by medical 
care, but also by access to food, supportive relationships, and opportunities to remain connected. 
• Meals can address a basic health need while also creating a natural opportunity for social connection. 
Social Participation 
• Meals were discussed as social functions, not simply food delivery. 
• Participants noted traditions such as senior-center potlucks, recipe swaps, neighborhood barbecues, and larger 
community potlucks. 
• There was interest in informal, welcoming, and potentially intergenerational gatherings centered around food and 
shared activity. 
• Possible ideas included neighborhood potlucks, community cookouts, recipe exchanges, and gatherings designed to 
reach people who may otherwise be socially isolated. 
Respect & Social Inclusion 
• The group emphasized belonging and connection, not just programming “for older adults.” 
• Participants discussed creating environments where people of different ages can interact naturally and where older 
residents remain visible, valued, and connected to the wider community. 
• Food-centered events were seen as one accessible way to bring together people who might not otherwise 
participate in the same activity. 
Civic Participation & Volunteerism 
• Volunteerism was discussed through the Heart of Maine initiative and Good Neighbor-type programs. 
• The conversation expanded beyond traditional, formal volunteering toward smaller and more informal ways 
residents can help one another. 
• A central question emerged: How do we make it easier for someone who wants to help to find someone who could 
use that help? 
• Participants considered whether a stronger culture of everyday helpfulness could complement existing volunteer 
programs. 
Outdoor Spaces & Public Places 
• Participants discussed how physical design can either encourage or discourage interaction. 
• The large swing in Pickering Square was cited as an example of a feature that invites people to linger, share space, 
and interact. 
• The group discussed whether some downtown streets could periodically be configured differently to create more 
social space. 
• One idea was to close Broad Street to cars during certain evening hours and use the space for gathering, dining, 
events, or other community activity. 
• The broader design question was: How can public spaces encourage people to stay, meet one another, and interact 
rather than simply move through them?
Bangor Livable Communities | Working Discussion Summary | September 2026 
 
 
 
Still to Explore 
• Complete discussion of the remaining Age-Friendly domains and identify where themes overlap. 
• Separate ideas that are already underway from new priorities for the updated plan. 
• Identify which ideas are best led by the City, community partners, volunteers, or shared efforts. 
• Translate recurring themes into a small number of clear, achievable goals and actions. 
• Potentially poll residents regarding their interest in these ideas in November.
